pr_title: Don't create xiaomi_miio sensors if inital state is None

<!--

For the xiaomi_miio platform, when None is returned by the devices the following 2 assumptions can be made of its meaning:
1. The requested data is unsupported. e.g. asking a vacuum without a mop the status of its mop.
2. Glitches in the matrix that makes the device return None for some unknown reason. 

This PR introduces changes to handle these 2 assumptions.

Honestly, I don't like this solution. I think we should just ignore the value if it's `None`. Like here https://github.com/home-assistant/core/pull/57197
What do you think about this solution https://github.com/home-assistant/core/compare/dev...bieniu:xiaomi_miio/none_value?expand=1

With your proposed solution, fetching data of unsupported features will go unnoticed because we are silencing the return of None. 

E.g. this will silence the issue where a vacuum that does not have a mop will still try and request if the mop is attached or not. And this will go completely unnoticed as the return `None` is silenced. I prefer to be explicit.

Essentially, returning `None` shouldn't be accepted as normal behavior for everything. It should be the other way around.

I would accept your solution if there is a warning added when unexpected None is returned. This brings us back to my solution.

Another solution would be to extend `XiaomiGenericSensor` for AirPurifiers and ignore None for all its sensors. But I do not agree that it should be ignored for everything(vacuums, fans, etc).
We can mark an entity as `unavailable` when the state is `None`. But if the device sends `None` for no reason, that's not a correct approach IMO. I think we need second opinion 😀
I added a comment to the issue: https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/57474#issuecomment-941581989

What does it mean when the device returns `None` as value. Does it mean there's a connection issue or that we don't know what the value is? If it's the latter we normally set state to `None` which will be translated to unknown state. Only when we know that the device is offline or similar should we set the state to unavailable.

I think we may need to do a larger refactor to handle this properly. The effects seem to be affecting multiple platforms and the current solution doesn't seem to scale well.

> What does it mean when the device returns None as value.

For these 2 attributes of `AirPurifier` specifically, just a small glitch in the matrix. Sometimes it can return `None`, then we will just mark it as unavailable as the sensor is in fact, unavailable. Until the device returns the right value again.

Using an "unknown" state could also work indeed.

In the case of Vacuums, 9/10 cases mean the feature is not supported. For this case, another PR will be opened once https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/57474#issuecomment-942025802 is fulfilled.

or shall this one be marked as unavailable?

A temporary None should just mean there is no update. To indicate a sensor is not available we can make in un-available, but only if we know what the behavior is. I agree with @jbouwh `None` states should be ignored.  The integration now updates data every 15 seconds so if the value `None` appears, for 15 seconds the entity should use the old state and then get the new one.

> My advice is to ignore None-states if the sensor is supported. A temporary None should just mean there is no update. To indicate a sensor is not available we can make in un-available, but only if we know what the behavior is

When `None` is returned as state, the entity will be marked as "Unknown State" by HA. 

@MartinHjelmare is against marking it as Unavailable, as this means that the device is unavailable, which is not true. The device is available, the state is just temp unknown due to the "known" None that is returned every now and then.

> I understand, but the way to approach this would be perhaps in the backend library, not here.

I agree, but i do not have such device in my possession to do proper testing and supply a proper fix to the lib. So a solution in HA is the quick win for now.

>  The integration now updates data every 15 seconds so if the value None appears, for 15 seconds the entity should use the old state and then get the new one.

So you are saying, if these attributes that are know to return None every now and then, to ignore the None and keep the previous state? And only update once a proper value is returned? @MartinHjelmare what do you think of this approach? Is it acceptable?
If it's a known quirk in the device we can ignore an update, yes.

So I've now made it so that, for know attributes that misbehave with none, the None is ignored for up to 3 updates. 

So, the state will be set to unknown if:
1. it was not previously unknown
2. failed to provide valid state after 3 tries 

Is this better? So now `allow_none_as_return_value` basically means, Its known that this attribute returns None every now and then and is handled accordingly. Instead of blindly "accepting" none for every attribute.

After doing some thinking on this, I'm fine with it if other reviewers agree, even when I don't like the solution. The reasons not to like this:
* Adding extra logic (counters, extra parameters to sensor definitions) will make the code more complicated by piling more logical decisions to the integration and will increase the maintenance burden
* I'm not (still) seeing what value the user is getting here (compared to simply suppressing on error cases)

To my understanding, there are two cases when the sensor state could be `None`:
1. The sensor returns `None` during the initial update. This happens most likely because the feature is not supported by the device
2. The sensor value "flaps" from a valid value to `None`. This is likely caused by some hardware failure

An alternative approach to fix the issue:
1. Log a warning on `None`s during initial update to let the user know that they should report incorrectly added entity (case "non-supported sensor"). This might result to some false positives, but I find it better than suppressing the fact that the device is not behaving as expected.
2. If the state unexpectedly changes to `None` (case "flapping sensor"), debug log it and use the existing value. If needed, we can try to find a solution for this case-by-case basis, but my personal opinion is that when other information is correctly reported by the device, the backend library should not interfere (or do forced updates or anything like that).

This way we can avoid adding new logic and sensor parameters while still avoiding spamming the log on occasional sensor failures. 

Opinions? Like @OGKevin, I'd really like to see this fixed by the next release when not even for a point release.

Yea, code gets complex when dealing with None/null. That is one of the side effects of having to deal with those values. Your proposed solutions would also add some level of complexity. Being able to properly tell the diff between None for the first time and None after receiving valid updates. I hate assumptions, your proposed solution assumes the reasoning for the None for all attributes and sensors. Where my approach is a little more specific. 

A good improvement would be for the lib to raise exceptions with proper meaning of what went wrong so that users of the lib do not have to assume the issue.

>I'm not (still) seeing what value the user is getting here

The biggest user value is user XP. For the devs: Instead of silently ignoring None's and marking sensors as unknown state, which is bad user XP, it gives the devs an explanation on why things are marked as unknown state and get the issue fixed. Another user benefit is that if the sensors is known to flap, the flapping will be dealt with by not setting the state to unknown.

The fact that these nones are getting logged we've learned:
* that some vacuums with mops do not support all mop related features/sensors
* some air purifiers have misbehaving apis.

By silently ignoring None, we would not have learned this and sensors would just randomly/always be marked as none without additional insights in logs.


> first none means that the sensor is not supported, which is not true

I think you didn't mention that `None` values show up for vacuum sensors. Why is this assumption not true?

For vacuums, None _can_ mean that its indeed an unsupported feature. In other words, unsupported feature is one of the reasons to return None for vacuums. However, there are some attributes that are unsupported  but can be determined via another attribute, which means the sensor can be created just fine. 

```
  is_water_box_attached=False
  is_water_box_carriage_attached=None
```

In this case (depending on the model) `is_water_box_carriage_attached=is_water_box_attached=False`.

This is why I will create a separate PR for vacuum's sensors so that:
1. There will be a proper mapping for sensors to be created for vacuum models, instead of blindly assuming that the None means unsupported.
2. for the vacuum models where the above example is the case, alter the sensor accordingly instead of dropping them.

To avoid complicating the issue any further with corner cases, I'm still hoping that we can get this fixed for the next release. My opinion how to handle this is still unchanged, but I'll try paraphrase the logic I'd like the integration to follow:
1. First update is performed during the setup, and sensor entities are created only for sensors that have a non-None value. If a `None` is reported, we log a warning.
2. If an update on a value for an existing sensor gets `None`, we consider that as a device glitch and discard it (while debug logging it, just in case someone is reading logs). 

> However, there are some attributes that are unsupported but can be determined via another attribute, which means the sensor can be created just fine.
